This analysis considers the first two aspects of the economic opportunity, but not the last, as it is likely to be circuit-specific and depend upon circuit planning and design. This aspect does, however, have the potential to obviate capital expenditure for voltage regulation equipment and corresponding maintenance expenses. To be cost-effective, such an SST would have to have a lower life cycle cost than the conventional transformer, rectifier, converters, and conventional transformer losses. For the purposes of this rough cost-benefit analysis, we need not know the initial cost of the DCFC power electronics or an SST and can assume them to be roughly equal. Likewise, we can assume the losses in the SST and DCFC power electronics to be roughly equivalent, but for possible small additional losses in the SST for an isolating rectifier. If the avoided cost of the low frequency iron core transformer and its losses allows for a margin in the cost of the SST such that it can include nominal additional cost of an isolating rectifier, multiple DC-to-DC converters and marginally higher power electronics losses due to the isolating conversion, the SST in this application should be cost-effective. This is the cost comparison that was made in this analysis. The assumed economic perspective of the analysis is that of a taxable entity such as an investor- owned utility experiencing the cost-benefit of ownership and operation and maintenance of the distribution system. The analysis took the results of the simulated scenarios and calculated economic effects and compared the economics of the scenarios. The analysis also calculated projected maintenance expense due to switching operations of switching and tap-change devices on the system.
